sources.text: When relying on Serializable transactions to prevent anomalies, it is important that any data read from a permanent user table not be considered valid until the transaction which read it has successfully committed. This is true even for read-only transactions, except that data read within a deferrable read-only transaction is known to be valid as soon as it is read, because such a transaction waits until it can acquire a snapshot guaranteed to be free from such problems before starting to read any data. In all other cases applications must not depend on results read during a transaction that later aborted; instead, they should retry the transaction until it succeeds.

Consistent use of Serializable transactions can simplify development. The guarantee that any set of successfully committed concurrent Serializable transactions will have the same effect as if they were run one at a time means that if you can demonstrate that a single transaction, as written, will do the right thing when run by itself, you can have confidence that it will do the right thing in any mix of Serializable transactions, even without any information about what those other transactions might do, or it will not successfully commit. It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies. The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure, but balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and SELECT FOR UPDATE or SELECT FOR SHARE, Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments.

13.5. Serialization Failure Handling #

Both Repeatable Read and Serializable isolation levels can produce errors that are designed to prevent serialization anomalies. As previously stated, applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions that fail due to serialization errors. Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code 40001 (serialization_failure).

In some cases it is also appropriate to retry unique-key failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23505 (unique_violation), and exclusion constraint failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23P01 (exclusion_violation). For example, if the application selects a new value for a primary key column after inspecting the currently stored keys, it could get a unique-key failure because another application instance selected the same new key concurrently. This is effectively a serialization failure, but the server will not detect it as such because it cannot “see” the connection between the inserted value and the previous reads. There are also some corner cases in which the server will issue a unique-key or exclusion constraint error even though in principle it has enough information to determine that a serialization problem is the underlying cause. While it's recommendable to just retry serialization_failure errors unconditionally, more care is needed when retrying these other error codes, since they might represent persistent error conditions rather than transient failures.

It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use. Therefore, PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility, since it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.

When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The second time through, the transaction will see the previously-committed change as part of its initial view of the database, so there is no logical conflict in using the new version of the row as the starting point for the new transaction's update.

Note that only updating transactions might need to be retried; read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts.

The Repeatable Read mode provides a rigorous guarantee that each transaction sees a completely stable view of the database. However, this view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level. For example, even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but not see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record. Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions.

response.evidence_note: The sources provide the necessary rules: retry the complete transaction including decision logic, retry serialization_failure (40001) unconditionally, and note unique-key failures after inspecting stored keys are effectively serialization failures; the source also notes PostgreSQL offers no automatic retry.

questions.stem:
A payroll service uses PostgreSQL Serializable transactions to assign employee badge numbers. The transaction performs:

Step 1. SELECT MAX(badge_number) FROM employees;
Step 2. Compute a new badge number in application code as MAX + 1;
Step 3. INSERT a new employee using that computed badge number;

The service runs multiple instances concurrently and has no automatic retry facility. A worker instance receives SQLSTATE 40001 during the INSERT after another instance already inserted the same MAX + 1 value and committed. The worker has not yet committed. The service's current retry wrapper only re-executes Step 3, the INSERT, with the same computed badge number. Under the supplied PostgreSQL rules, what is the defensible design decision?

Condition 1: The error is SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure).
Condition 2: The SELECT in Step 1 is a read from a permanent user table.
Condition 3: The application computes the badge number from that read, not from a constant.
Condition 4: The retry wrapper currently repeats only the INSERT with the same computed value.
Condition 5: The value computed before the failure may have been based on data the transaction read before it aborted; another committed transaction may have already inserted that value.
Condition 6: PostgreSQL does not provide automatic retry.

Which option best evaluates the design after this serialization failure?
options: Retry only the INSERT with the same value, because SQLSTATE 40001 guarantees the INSERT itself was not applied.
Retry the complete transaction from the beginning, including recomputing the badge number from a fresh SELECT, because the original read is not valid until commit and PostgreSQL does not auto-retry.
Retry only the INSERT after looking up whether the same badge number now exists, because the source states read-only transactions never have serialization conflicts.
Abort permanently, because a SQLSTATE 40001 on an INSERT is always a persistent data error rather than a serialization failure.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: the source says data read from a permanent user table is not valid until the reading transaction commits, so retry the whole transaction from the beginning and re-derive values from the new initial view. Option A is wrong because 40001 does not validate pre-failure reads and the source says to retry the complete transaction including logic that decides which SQL or values to use. Option C is wrong because the read-only statement applies to read-only transactions, not this read-then-insert transaction. Option D is wrong because 40001 is the serialization_failure code and should be retried unconditionally.
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must combine PostgreSQL serialization-failure semantics with the read-then-write dependency created by computing a badge number from MAX. They must evaluate four retry designs under concrete constraints: invalid pre-commit reads, unconditional 40001 retry, full-transaction retry including decision logic, and no automatic retry facility.

expected_steps: Recognize that the SELECT MAX result is not valid until the transaction commits, so the computed badge number may be stale.
Identify that SQLSTATE 40001 is a serialization failure that should be retried rather than treated as persistent.
Apply the rule to retry the whole transaction, including recomputing the badge number from a fresh SELECT.
Reject the partial retry because it reuses a value derived from pre-abort reads.

questions.stem:
A payroll service uses PostgreSQL Serializable transactions to assign employee badge numbers. The transaction performs:

Step 1. SELECT MAX(badge_number) FROM employees;
Step 2. Compute a new badge number in application code as MAX + 1;
Step 3. INSERT a new employee using that computed badge number;

The service runs multiple instances concurrently and has no automatic retry facility. A worker instance receives SQLSTATE 40001 during the INSERT after another instance already inserted the same MAX + 1 value and committed. The worker has not yet committed. The service's current retry wrapper only re-executes Step 3, the INSERT, with the same computed badge number. Under the supplied PostgreSQL rules, what is the defensible design decision?

Condition 1: The error is SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure).
Condition 2: The SELECT in Step 1 is a read from a permanent user table.
Condition 3: The application computes the badge number from that read, not from a constant.
Condition 4: The retry wrapper currently repeats only the INSERT with the same computed value.
Condition 5: The value computed before the failure may have been based on data the transaction read before it aborted; another committed transaction may have already inserted that value.
Condition 6: PostgreSQL does not provide automatic retry.

Which option best evaluates the design after this serialization failure?
options: Retry only the INSERT with the same value, because SQLSTATE 40001 guarantees the INSERT itself was not applied.
Retry the complete transaction from the beginning, including recomputing the badge number from a fresh SELECT, because the original read is not valid until commit and PostgreSQL does not auto-retry.
Retry only the INSERT after looking up whether the same badge number now exists, because the source states read-only transactions never have serialization conflicts.
Abort permanently, because a SQLSTATE 40001 on an INSERT is always a persistent data error rather than a serialization failure.
questions.explanation: Option B is correct: the source says data read from a permanent user table is not valid until the reading transaction commits, so retry the whole transaction from the beginning and re-derive values from the new initial view. Option A is wrong because 40001 does not validate pre-failure reads and the source says to retry the complete transaction including logic that decides which SQL or values to use. Option C is wrong because the read-only statement applies to read-only transactions, not this read-then-insert transaction. Option D is wrong because 40001 is the serialization_failure code and should be retried unconditionally.

They must evaluate four retry designs under concrete constraints: invalid pre-commit reads, unconditional 40001 retry, full-transaction retry including decision logic, and no automatic retry facility.

questions.stem:
An application uses PostgreSQL Serializable transactions. To create an item, a transaction executes `SELECT max(id) FROM items` to choose the next item id, and then inserts a row with that id. Another instance can run the same select-then-insert at the same time.

1. The application does not use a deferrable read-only transaction.
2. On a concurrent insert of the same id, PostgreSQL can return SQLSTATE `23505` (unique_violation) instead of `40001` (serialization_failure).
3. The `23505` error may be either transient or a persistent condition, so it cannot be retried with the same confidence as `40001`.
4. A correct retry must rerun the complete transaction, including the logic that chose the id, not just the failed INSERT.

Which statement best evaluates the application's retry design?
options: It should treat the `23505` as a serialization failure and retry the entire transaction only if the chosen id is still absent after re-reading it.
It should retry only the failed INSERT; because the id was read during the same transaction, a `40001` is impossible and the `23505` is always a serialization failure.
It should stop retrying on any `23505` because unique-key failures are always persistent and never effectively serialization failures.
It should rerun the whole transaction including the id-selection logic, but distinguish transient `23505` cases from persistent ones rather than retrying them unconditionally.
questions.explanation: The application reads permanent table data to choose a key and then writes. The supplied material says such reads are not valid until the transaction commits, and when a read decides a later write, applications must retry the whole transaction rather than just the failed statement. The source specifically notes that a select-then-insert could get a `23505` caused by another instance choosing the same key, which is effectively a serialization failure the server cannot detect, but it also warns that `23505` may represent a persistent error condition, so a blanket unconditional retry is less safe than for `40001`. Option D correctly reruns the complete transaction yet handles `23505` with more care than `40001`. Option A wrongly makes retry conditional on a re-read and mistreats the failure class. Option B wrongly retries only the INSERT and wrongly says `40001` is impossible. Option C wrongly treats all `23505` failures as persistent.
questions.difficulty_reason: The student must combine the rule that reads feeding later writes are not trustworthy until commit, the retry-the-whole-transaction rule, and the source's distinction between unconditional retry of `40001` and careful handling of `23505`. Choosing option D requires evaluating why `23505` can be a hidden serialization failure yet cannot be retried with the same confidence, while rejecting the superficially plausible but wrong alternatives.

expected_steps: Recognize that reads from permanent tables used to select a key are not valid until the transaction commits.
Identify that a concurrent select-then-insert can cause a 23505 that is effectively a serialization failure.
Apply the rule that retry must rerun the complete transaction, including the id-selection logic.
Evaluate that 23505 may be persistent, so it should not be retried unconditionally like 40001.

questions.stem:
An application uses PostgreSQL Serializable transactions. To create an item, a transaction executes `SELECT max(id) FROM items` to choose the next item id, and then inserts a row with that id. Another instance can run the same select-then-insert at the same time.

1. The application does not use a deferrable read-only transaction.
2. On a concurrent insert of the same id, PostgreSQL can return SQLSTATE `23505` (unique_violation) instead of `40001` (serialization_failure).
3. The `23505` error may be either transient or a persistent condition, so it cannot be retried with the same confidence as `40001`.
4. A correct retry must rerun the complete transaction, including the logic that chose the id, not just the failed INSERT.

Which statement best evaluates the application's retry design?
options: It should treat the `23505` as a serialization failure and retry the entire transaction only if the chosen id is still absent after re-reading it.
It should retry only the failed INSERT; because the id was read during the same transaction, a `40001` is impossible and the `23505` is always a serialization failure.
It should stop retrying on any `23505` because unique-key failures are always persistent and never effectively serialization failures.
It should rerun the whole transaction including the id-selection logic, but distinguish transient `23505` cases from persistent ones rather than retrying them unconditionally.
questions.explanation: The application reads permanent table data to choose a key and then writes. The supplied material says such reads are not valid until the transaction commits, and when a read decides a later write, applications must retry the whole transaction rather than just the failed statement. The source specifically notes that a select-then-insert could get a `23505` caused by another instance choosing the same key, which is effectively a serialization failure the server cannot detect, but it also warns that `23505` may represent a persistent error condition, so a blanket unconditional retry is less safe than for `40001`. Option D correctly reruns the complete transaction yet handles `23505` with more care than `40001`. Option A wrongly makes retry conditional on a re-read and mistreats the failure class. Option B wrongly retries only the INSERT and wrongly says `40001` is impossible. Option C wrongly treats all `23505` failures as persistent.
questions.difficulty_reason: The student must combine the rule that reads feeding later writes are not trustworthy until commit, the retry-the-whole-transaction rule, and the source's distinction between unconditional retry of `40001` and careful handling of `23505`. Choosing option D requires evaluating why `23505` can be a hidden serialization failure yet cannot be retried with the same confidence, while rejecting the superficially plausible but wrong alternatives.

questions.stem:
An application runs under Serializable isolation. One transaction does the following: it reads the current maximum value of a primary key column, computes the next value in application code, and inserts a row using that computed value. The transaction then fails with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure).

Consider this proposed retry design:

1. The retry loop catches only SQLSTATE 40001.
2. On that error it aborts the current transaction.
3. It then re-executes only the INSERT statement, reusing the primary key value computed before the failure.
4. It treats a resulting SQLSTATE 23505 (unique_violation) from that INSERT as a permanent error and stops retrying.

Which evaluation of this design is best supported by the course evidence?
options: The design is mostly correct; reusing the computed key is safe because retrying only the INSERT rechecks the uniqueness constraint against current data.

The design is flawed: the retry must re-run the whole transaction, including the reads and key-selection logic, and applications may also need to retry some unique-key failures such as 23505, which may be effectively serialization failures.
The design is correct for Serializable because 40001 is the only code that can indicate a serialization problem, and 23505 always represents a persistent error that should never be retried.
The design is flawed only in that it aborts the transaction; retrying the INSERT without aborting would preserve the earlier read results and avoid any serialization conflict.
questions.explanation:
The evidence states that it is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and which values to use, and that PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility because it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.
The read maximum value and the computed key are part of that logic, so re-executing only the INSERT with the previously computed key does not satisfy the requirement to retry the whole transaction.
The evidence also says it is appropriate in some cases to retry unique-key failures with SQLSTATE 23505, for example when the application selects a new primary key value after inspecting currently stored keys and another instance selected the same value concurrently; this is effectively a serialization failure even though the server does not detect it as such.
Option A is wrong because reusing the computed key does not replay the decision logic and the design fails to handle the relevant 23505 case.
Option C is wrong because 23505 is not always a persistent error and can be effectively a serialization failure.
Option D is wrong because the evidence directs the application to abort the current transaction on this error and retry the whole transaction from the beginning.
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must connect several constraints: a serialization failure on a transaction whose read determines a later write, the rule to retry the complete transaction including decision logic, the possible need to retry unique-key failures such as 23505, and the requirement to abort before retrying. The stem presents a concrete retry design and asks the learner to evaluate it by combining these interacting conditions, rather than simply restating the definition of serialization failure.

expected_steps: Identify that the transaction's read of the maximum key determines the later insert and is part of the transaction logic, so it must be included in the retry.
Recall that the application must abort the current transaction on a serialization failure and retry the whole transaction from the beginning.
Recognize that 23505 can be effectively a serialization failure when the key was selected after inspecting current keys, so it may need to be retried rather than treated as permanent.
Evaluate each option: reject designs that retry only the INSERT, treat 23505 as always permanent, or skip aborting the transaction.

questions.stem:
An application runs under Serializable isolation. One transaction does the following: it reads the current maximum value of a primary key column, computes the next value in application code, and inserts a row using that computed value. The transaction then fails with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization_failure).

Consider this proposed retry design:

1. The retry loop catches only SQLSTATE 40001.
2. On that error it aborts the current transaction.
3. It then re-executes only the INSERT statement, reusing the primary key value computed before the failure.
4. It treats a resulting SQLSTATE 23505 (unique_violation) from that INSERT as a permanent error and stops retrying.

Which evaluation of this design is best supported by the course evidence?
options: The design is mostly correct; reusing the computed key is safe because retrying only the INSERT rechecks the uniqueness constraint against current data.

The design is flawed: the retry must re-run the whole transaction, including the reads and key-selection logic, and applications may also need to retry some unique-key failures such as 23505, which may be effectively serialization failures.
The design is correct for Serializable because 40001 is the only code that can indicate a serialization problem, and 23505 always represents a persistent error that should never be retried.
The design is flawed only in that it aborts the transaction; retrying the INSERT without aborting would preserve the earlier read results and avoid any serialization conflict.
questions.explanation:
The evidence states that it is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and which values to use, and that PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility because it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.
The read maximum value and the computed key are part of that logic, so re-executing only the INSERT with the previously computed key does not satisfy the requirement to retry the whole transaction.
The evidence also says it is appropriate in some cases to retry unique-key failures with SQLSTATE 23505, for example when the application selects a new primary key value after inspecting currently stored keys and another instance selected the same value concurrently; this is effectively a serialization failure even though the server does not detect it as such.
Option A is wrong because reusing the computed key does not replay the decision logic and the design fails to handle the relevant 23505 case.
Option C is wrong because 23505 is not always a persistent error and can be effectively a serialization failure.
Option D is wrong because the evidence directs the application to abort the current transaction on this error and retry the whole transaction from the beginning.

sources.text: When relying on Serializable transactions to prevent anomalies, it is important that any data read from a permanent user table not be considered valid until the transaction which read it has successfully committed. This is true even for read-only transactions, except that data read within a deferrable read-only transaction is known to be valid as soon as it is read, because such a transaction waits until it can acquire a snapshot guaranteed to be free from such problems before starting to read any data. In all other cases applications must not depend on results read during a transaction that later aborted; instead, they should retry the transaction until it succeeds.

Consistent use of Serializable transactions can simplify development. The guarantee that any set of successfully committed concurrent Serializable transactions will have the same effect as if they were run one at a time means that if you can demonstrate that a single transaction, as written, will do the right thing when run by itself, you can have confidence that it will do the right thing in any mix of Serializable transactions, even without any information about what those other transactions might do, or it will not successfully commit. It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies. The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure, but balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and SELECT FOR UPDATE or SELECT FOR SHARE, Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments.

13.5. Serialization Failure Handling #

Both Repeatable Read and Serializable isolation levels can produce errors that are designed to prevent serialization anomalies. As previously stated, applications using these levels must be prepared to retry transactions that fail due to serialization errors. Such an error's message text will vary according to the precise circumstances, but it will always have the SQLSTATE code 40001 (serialization_failure).

In some cases it is also appropriate to retry unique-key failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23505 (unique_violation), and exclusion constraint failures, which have SQLSTATE code 23P01 (exclusion_violation). For example, if the application selects a new value for a primary key column after inspecting the currently stored keys, it could get a unique-key failure because another application instance selected the same new key concurrently. This is effectively a serialization failure, but the server will not detect it as such because it cannot “see” the connection between the inserted value and the previous reads. There are also some corner cases in which the server will issue a unique-key or exclusion constraint error even though in principle it has enough information to determine that a serialization problem is the underlying cause. While it's recommendable to just retry serialization_failure errors unconditionally, more care is needed when retrying these other error codes, since they might represent persistent error conditions rather than transient failures.

It is important to retry the complete transaction, including all logic that decides which SQL to issue and/or which values to use. Therefore, PostgreSQL does not offer an automatic retry facility, since it cannot do so with any guarantee of correctness.

When an application receives this error message, it should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning. The second time through, the transaction will see the previously-committed change as part of its initial view of the database, so there is no logical conflict in using the new version of the row as the starting point for the new transaction's update.

Note that only updating transactions might need to be retried; read-only transactions will never have serialization conflicts.

The Repeatable Read mode provides a rigorous guarantee that each transaction sees a completely stable view of the database. However, this view will not necessarily always be consistent with some serial (one at a time) execution of concurrent transactions of the same level. For example, even a read-only transaction at this level may see a control record updated to show that a batch has been completed but not see one of the detail records which is logically part of the batch because it read an earlier revision of the control record. Attempts to enforce business rules by transactions running at this isolation level are not likely to work correctly without careful use of explicit locks to block conflicting transactions.
